title: Form changes follow the same route in individual development and racial history

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Form changes follow the same route in individual development and racial history

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Changes of form produced by varying rates of growth are the same phenomenon in individual development and in the differences between species; a transformation from one form to another follows the same course whether it happens within a lifetime or over ancestral history, which accounts for much of von Baer's law of recapitulation.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: From one form, or ratio of magnitude, to another there is but one straight and direct road of transformation, be the journey taken fast or slow; and if the transformation take place at all, it will in all likelihood proceed in the self-same way, whether it occur within the life-time of an individual or during the long ancestral history of a race.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Conclusion and summary”. Scope: ontogeny and phylogeny of organic form

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-35: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.50

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern geometric morphometrics gives the claim measurable trajectory predictions. Public specimens allow strong tests in selected clades, but ancestral inference and limited ontogenetic series prevent resolving the universal statement.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Represent ontogenetic and phylogenetic shape changes in a common morphometric space and compare their trajectories, directions, and ordering of landmarks. Support requires phylogenetic transformations to follow the same paths as within-individual development more often than null or alternative developmental models predict.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ancestral forms must be inferred rather than observed.

The universal 'one road' formulation is much broader than available clade datasets.

Heterochrony can mimic shared paths.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.4
discriminating power: 0.45
analysis feasibility: 0.4
data existence: 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Geometric morphometrics can test whether individual development and species differences follow the same shape path, and both scans and trees are public. Usable ontogenetic series are a minority of what is archived, so the test is a restricted-scope one. Even then, a straight path in a reduced shape space is only a partial discriminator from other growth rules that pass through similar intermediates.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In a shape space, compare the trajectory of an ontogenetic series with the trajectory connecting the same forms along a phylogeny. A shared path, within a stated tolerance, would support one road of transformation; ontogenies that bend away from the phylogenetic path would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Most scans are adults, so ontogenetic series have to be assembled clade by clade.

Coverage is strong for a few vertebrate groups and weak for the stated scope of organic form.

Shared allometry can make ontogeny and phylogeny look alike in a low-dimensional shape space.

fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.4
data existence: 0.6
discriminating power: 0.5
analysis feasibility: 0.5
